qt: to the Commission Lukas Mandl (PPE) Subject:

According to a Eurostat study, in 2020, barely over 60% of those aged 65-74 from across the EU reported using the internet in the past three months. The internet and digital services are playing an ever greater role in society and increasingly supplanting analogue resources and services. While there is no denying the efficiency gain that comes with this shift, older generations – in which some people are unacquainted with new technologies – must not be forgotten. 1.
What steps is the Commission taking to enable less digitally skilled older people to also play an active part in modern society?
What measures are in the pipeline to support older people with administrative matters and everyday tasks?
What can be done to avoid the social isolation of older people and ageism as a result of the increasing emphasis on the digital space?
at: (English version) to the Commission Lukas Mandl (PPE) (27 February 2024) Subject: Participation in society of digitally inexperienced older people According to a Eurostat study, in 2020, barely over 60% of those aged 65-74 from across the EU reported using the Internet in the past three months. The Internet and digital services are playing an ever greater role in society and increasingly supplanting analogue resources and services. While there is no denying the efficiency gain that comes with this shift, older generations — in which some people are unacquainted with new technologies — must not be forgotten. 1. What steps is the Commission taking to enable less digitally skilled older people to also play an active part in modern society? 2.
What measures are in the pipeline to support older people with administrative matters and everyday tasks?

3. What can be done to avoid the social isolation of older people and ageism as a result of the increasing emphasis on the digital space? (4 June 2024) Digital technologies can enable people to stay in control of their lives and continue to contribute to the economy and society as they age. The Green Paper on Ageing (2021) (1) stressed the importance of enhancing older adults’ digital skills, to allow them to participate in society. The European Skills Agenda (2020-2025) (2) envisages that, by 2025, 70% of adults (between 16 and 74 years old) should have at least basic digital skills. The Digital Decade Policy Programme (3) sets the target to have 80% of European adults with basic digital skills by 203 0 (4). In this context, the Horizon Europe coordination and support action Improving Digital Empowerment for Active and Healthy Living (IDEAHL) (5) is developing a concept for an EU digital health literacy strategy. In its Demography Toolbox Communication (6), the Commission highlighted that Europe needs to build a ‘longevity society’ that values the longer lifetime spent in older age, empowers older citizens, and nurtures the welfare and well-being of present and future generations alike. The Horizon Europe call on the Silver Deal (7) aims to support digitally enabled person-centred health and care solutions for active and healthy living, including administrative tasks (8). The Union of Equality strategies (9) stress the need to combat stereotypes and fight age-based discrimination (10) within their respective remit, and give everyone equal chances to contribute and thrive, including by harnessing the potential of technology. In this framework, the High-level group on non-discrimination, equality and diversit y (11) promotes exchanges of practices on age equality and combating ageism and will publish an output paper in 2024.
